llm.limitations_zh: 摘要未提及

title: Omics-derived signatures in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease: from molecular characterization to clinical translation.
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is a highly prevalent systemic metabolic disorder with heterogeneous clinical trajectories. Although liver biopsy remains the histological reference standard, its invasiveness and limited scalability restrict routine use, while established non-invasive tests mainly capture fibrosis-related structural changes and provide limited insight into molecular heterogeneity, active steatohepatitis and early fibrotic transition. Multi-omics technologies offer a mechanistically informed framework for resolving this heterogeneity. In this Review, we summarize recent advances in genomic, transcriptomic, single-cell and spatial, proteomic, lipidomic and metabolomic signatures and candidate biomarkers in MASLD. Genomic studies define inherited susceptibility and risk enrichment, whereas transcriptomic and spatial approaches reveal disease-associated pathways, cell states and tissue niches. Proteomics provides blood-accessible signals of steatohepatitis activity, matrix remodelling and systemic metabolic risk, while lipidomics and metabolomics capture lipotoxic lipid composition, mitochondrial stress, bile acid dysregulation and gut-liver metabolic perturbation. We further discuss how integrative multi-omics, systems biology and artificial intelligence can organize high-dimensional molecular data into disease modules, molecular subtypes, biomarker signatures and candidate therapeutic nodes. In addition, omics-informed studies of bioactive compounds and precision nutrition illustrate how nutritional modulation may be evaluated through molecular response profiles. Despite promising progress, most omics-derived biomarkers remain limited by cohort specificity, platform dependence, incomplete external validation and unclear clinical thresholds. Future translation will require longitudinal, spatially resolved and clinically anchored integration to support risk stratification, at-risk metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis detection, fibrosis assessment, treatment-response prediction and precision medicine in MASLD.
affiliations: Department of Hepatobiliary and Pancreatic Surgery, General Surgery Center, the First Hospital of Jilin University, Changchun, Jilin, China.
Department of Hepatology and Gastroenterology, Charité-Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Campus Virchow-Klinikum (CVK) and Campus Charité Mitte (CCM), Berlin, Germany.

llm.novelty_zh: 综述性质，系统梳理MASLD的多组学标志物及其临床转化路径，无新方法。
llm.summary_zh: 该综述总结了MASLD在基因组、转录组、单细胞与空间、蛋白组、脂质组和代谢组层面的分子特征与候选生物标志物。文章还讨论了多组学与AI在疾病分型与风险分层中的整合思路。
llm.why_it_matters_zh: 为肝脏脂肪性疾病的分子分型与无创诊断研究提供了系统参考。
llm.limitations_zh: 多数生物标志物受队列特异性、平台依赖和外部验证不足的限制，临床阈值尚不明确。

title: Deciphering isonicotinylation and mast cell-associated pathogenic patterns in Duchenne muscular dystrophy: evidence from ensemble learning-driven multi-omics and in vitro validation
abstract: Background: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is dystrophin-deficiency skeletal and cardiac muscle disease. Protein post-translational modification (PTM) and aberrant immune cell activation play a key role in its pathogenesis. Objective: Our study aims to investigate isonicotinylation (Kinic)-associated signature modulatory patterns in mast cells and DMD pathogenesis. Methods: We first performed integrated bioinformatic methods, such as WGCNA, GSVA, and CIBERSORT to identify Kinic and mast cell (KM)-related differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in DMD patient muscle bulk profiles (GSE38417 and GSE109178). Next, consensus clustering and assembling machine learning pipeline identified KM-associated diagnostic model and molecular subgroups in training the DMD patient muscle bulk set (GSE6011), and then, diagnostic model performance was examined in the independent DMD patient muscle bulk set (GSE32720). In addition, SHAP analysis decoded the main contributor in KM-associated diagnostic model construction, and contributor molecular and immune characters in DMD were estimated in GSE6011 and the DMD mouse muscle single-cell transcriptomic dataset (GSE213925) assisted by computational virtual cells. In addition, the deep learning framework and network pharmacology identified the drug synergy strategy for the treatment of DMD. Finally, the in vitro assay identified expression patterns of the main contributor. Results: KM-associated molecular patterns can potentially guide the diagnostic and molecular stratification for DMD patients. USP18 can be considered an upregulated and mast cell-distributed hub gene involved in pathogenesis of DMD. In addition, finafloxacin with BRD-K10482608 can be considered two potential therapeutic candidates for DMD patient clinical applications. Conclusion: Our investigation described a novel forecasting and therapeutic model for DMD patients, which potentially enhances DMD patient clinical translation.

title: Bone morphogenetic protein 4 meets artificial intelligence: a comprehensive review of AI-driven advances in drug discovery, structural modeling, and clinical translation.
abstract: Background Bone Morphogenetic Protein 4 (BMP4), a member of the transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) superfamily, plays pivotal roles in embryonic development, tissue homeostasis, and disease pathogenesis-including cancer, fibrosis, and fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP). The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methodologies over the past 5 years has created unprecedented opportunities for understanding and therapeutically targeting BMP4 biology at multiple scales, from atomic-resolution structure prediction to population-level clinical prognostication. Objective This review systematically examines the intersection of BMP4 biology and AI across three core domains: (1) AI-driven drug discovery targeting BMP4 signaling pathways, (2) deep learning-based protein structure prediction and computational modeling of BMP4 and its receptor complexes, and (3) clinical AI applications for BMP4-associated diseases. Methods A narrative review with systematic search elements was conducted across PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, bioRxiv, and arXiv for English-language publications from 2020 to 2026, supplemented by targeted searches via Semantic Scholar. Included studies were categorized as BMP4-specific, BMP receptor/BMP-pathway-targeted, or transferable AI methodology not yet applied to BMP4. Results We find that AI has accelerated BMP4-related research along multiple axes, though with important caveats. AlphaFold3 and related tools have generated high-confidence predicted models of BMP4-receptor complex architecture, aspects of which were previously intractable to experimental structure determination; these predictions remain to be fully validated experimentally. ML-guided virtual screening has identified first-in-class BMP pathway (receptor) modulators for FOP, although BMP4-specific small-molecule modulators have not yet been identified computationally. Single-cell transcriptomics combined with machine learning have revealed BMP4's context-dependent roles in glioblastoma cell state transitions and cancer-associated fibroblast biology; and LASSO-Cox regression models incorporating BMP4 expression have shown promising prognostic value in pancreatic adenocarcinoma and gastric cancer, pending prospective validation. Significant gaps persist-most notably the absence of BMP4-specific de novo protein design efforts, the scarcity of large-scale training datasets for BMP4-targeted drug discovery, and the limited integration of multimodal AI approaches in BMP4 clinical research. Conclusion The convergence of BMP4 biology and AI represents a fertile research Frontier. While foundational tools are now in place, realizing the full translational potential of AI-augmented BMP4 research will require coordinated efforts in data generation, model development, and rigorous experimental and clinical validation. We outline priority directions for the next 5 years (approximately 2026-2031).

title: Integrative transcriptomics reveals an ECM/PNN-high astrocyte state and cross-tissue biomarkers in major depressive disorder
abstract: Background: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is associated with impaired neural plasticity, while extracellular matrix (ECM) and perineuronal nets (PNNs) are important regulators of synaptic stability and extracellular homeostasis. However, the cellular states and molecular signatures associated with ECM/PNN alterations in MDD remain poorly understood. Methods: We integrated bulk and single-cell transcriptomic datasets to characterize ECM/PNN-associated cellular states in MDD. Astrocyte populations were evaluated using multiple ECM/PNN scoring approaches, and disease-associated transcriptional changes were integrated with astrocyte co-expression networks to identify candidate molecular signatures. Functional enrichment, cell-cell communication, pseudotime, and in silico perturbation analyses were further used to investigate their biological context. Finally, corticosterone (CORT)-treated HT22 cells were used as a glucocorticoid-induced neuronal stress paradigm to assess stress-responsive expression of the identified genes. Results: Among astrocyte clusters, Cluster2 exhibited overall high ECM and PNN signature scores. Integration of Cluster2-associated co-expression modules with MDD-related differentially expressed genes identified 28 overlapping genes, from which ACSL6, FIP1L1, and ZNF709 were prioritized as cross-tissue candidate signatures showing consistent expression trends in brain and peripheral blood datasets. ACSL6 and ZNF709 were downregulated, whereas FIP1L1 was upregulated in MDD. Functional analyses implicated the three genes in metabolic and amino-acid-related processes, while FIP1L1 showed additional associations with cell adhesion, cytoskeletal organization, and synaptic signaling. Cell communication and pseudotime analyses further suggested altered intercellular signaling and increasing ECM/PNN activity across inferred astrocyte state transitions. In CORT-treated HT22 cells, ACSL6 and ZNF709 were significantly decreased, whereas FIP1L1 was increased, consistent with the transcriptomic observations. Conclusion: These findings identify an ECM/PNN-high astrocyte state and three associated cross-tissue molecular signatures in MDD. Among them, FIP1L1 emerged as a functionally prioritized candidate linked to adhesion- and synaptic-plasticity-related programs. The stress-responsive expression of these genes provides additional experimental support for their relevance to glucocorticoid-associated neuronal stress and supports an astrocyte-centered ECM/PNN working model for further mechanistic investigation.

title: Single-cell and spatial multi-omics for studying cell competition in the tumor microenvironment.
abstract: Cell competition is a conserved fitness-surveillance process, first described in Drosophila epithelia, by which cells compare relative fitness with their neighbors so that less-fit "loser" cells are eliminated, extruded or forced to differentiate while fitter "winner" cells expand. In the tumor microenvironment (TME), this logic appears to be co-opted by transformed clones that eliminate normal epithelium, outcompete neighboring subclones and reshape stromal and immune compartments, making cell competition a potentially underappreciated contributor to cancer clonal evolution, immune escape and therapy resistance. Because competition is defined by a comparison between adjacent cells and by a demonstrated change in the relative representation of one population, it is difficult to resolve with bulk sequencing, which averages across precisely the heterogeneity that defines it. The convergence of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), spatial transcriptomics, spatial and single-cell proteomics, artificial intelligence (AI) and network-inference bioinformatics now allows competition-relevant cellular states, interfaces and signaling relationships to be measured at the resolution the problem requires. We emphasize at the outset that these technologies are, in almost all current applications, hypothesis-generating: they identify candidate competitive interfaces and putative winner and loser states from static measurements, and they do not by themselves demonstrate that competition has occurred. This review synthesizes advances across these domains; proposes an explicit three-tier evidence framework separating direct experimental evidence of cell competition from competition-relevant associations and from computational predictions; distinguishes cell competition from related processes such as clonal selection, immune editing and differential proliferation; and defines a putative cell competition network as a falsifiable construct whose edges include ligand-receptor, spatial-adjacency, metabolic and mechanical relations. We further outline a conceptual, context-dependent Cell Competition Score (CCS) as a testable specification rather than a biomarker-ready instrument, and set out the benchmarking, causal-inference and prospective-validation requirements that stand between current capability and any clinical application.

title: Identification of metabolic vulnerabilities and synthetic lethal targets utilizing artificial intelligence-driven precision medicine
abstract: Cancer metabolism is highly plastic, and most attempts to turn that plasticity into a therapeutic target fail for a specific, recurring reason: a computational prediction of a metabolic vulnerability is not the same evidentiary object as an experimentally confirmed one, and the two are routinely discussed as if they were interchangeable. This review takes that distinction as its starting point rather than its conclusion. Artificial intelligence and genome-scale systems biology have made it easy to generate metabolic hypotheses at a scale no experimental program could match - machine learning models trained on genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic data now output candidate vulnerabilities, biomarkers, and drug combinations faster than they can be tested - but the resulting literature has not been consistently honest about how far any given prediction has actually traveled toward clinical relevance. We examine six areas where this gap is most visible: multi-omics data integration, genome-scale metabolic network modeling, computational discovery of metabolic vulnerabilities and synthetic lethal interactions, single-cell and spatial resolution of metabolic heterogeneity, AI-guided drug and biomarker discovery, and the small set of studies that have actually reached clinical testing. Rather than summarizing these areas as separate literatures, we grade every substantive finding discussed against an explicit four-tier evidence standard - associative, mechanistic, perturbation-validated, or clinically tested - and we apply that standard critically rather than deferentially: several widely cited computational vulnerabilities remain unconfirmed outside the cell lines in which they were discovered, genome-scale models continue to carry unresolved gaps in reaction coverage that limit their predictive reach, and, of the AI-derived metabolic predictions discussed in this review, only one has so far been tested in a completed prospective clinical trial. We argue that this shortage of prospective validation, not a shortage of computational sophistication, is the field's central constraint, and we close by identifying where methodological effort would do the most good: standardized validation reporting, tissue-resolved rather than bulk metabolic models, and closer coupling between computational prediction and the specific experimental designs capable of falsifying it.

title: Integrating multi-omics with machine learning: from genomic variant functional annotation to pharmacogenomics and biomarker discovery.
abstract: Integrating heterogeneous multi-omics data with machine learning (ML) provides a powerful framework for interpreting genomic variants and advancing pharmacogenomic research in precision medicine. High-throughput technologies have generated vast datasets spanning genomics, transcriptomics, epigenomics, and proteomics, yet integrating these high-dimensional data into clinically meaningful insights remains a major computational challenge. Machine learning and deep learning models, including Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), Transformers, and Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), offer promising solutions. This narrative review provides a state-of-the-art overview of ML-driven multi-omics integration across early, intermediate, and late fusion paradigms. We highlight how these approaches may support functional variant interpretation, including the reclassification of Variants of Uncertain Significance (VUS), and emerging pharmacogenomic applications. Key areas include predictive biomarkers for drug efficacy, therapeutic resistance in precision oncology, and personalized dosing in rare and complex diseases. Finally, we discuss challenges related to data heterogeneity, clinical interpretability, and regulatory approval, as well as the requirements for translating emerging computational approaches into clinically validated pharmacogenomic practice and precision pharmacotherapy.

title: MGCF-Net: a multi-view granular-ball contrastive fusion network for spatial transcriptomics clustering.
abstract: Introduction Spatial domain identification from spatial transcriptomics (ST) data is essential for characterizing the spatial organization of complex tissues. Existing contrastive learning methods face a persistent trade-off: instance-level approaches are susceptible to false negatives, whereas cluster-level methods may overlook fine-grained local structures. Moreover, direct multi-view fusion may introduce redundant or noisy correlations, thereby degrading representation quality. Methods To address these limitations, we propose MGCF-Net, a multi-view granular-ball contrastive fusion network for spatial domain identification. MGCF-Net constructs a spatial graph and a feature graph to represent physical proximity and transcriptomic similarity, respectively. A redundancy-reduction objective preserves spot-level correspondence across the two views while suppressing spurious similarities between different spots. Multi-view granular-ball contrastive learning groups spot-level representations into local structural units and aligns them across views according to their membership overlap. Results On eight dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) tissue sections, MGCF-Net attains the highest mean adjusted Rand index (ARI) among the evaluated methods. Its normalized mutual information (NMI) remains competitive with the comparison methods. Discussion By contrasting local structural units rather than individual spots, MGCF-Net reduces the influence of false negatives arising from instance-level contrastive learning. This group-level formulation preserves coherent spatial structures without requiring a generative decoder.

title: Operationalizing the physiological state (P) in nonlinear behavioral systems: a measurement framework for state-dependent dynamics
abstract: Behavioral outcomes may vary within the same individual even when measured environmental conditions appear comparable. To test whether an organism's changing physiological condition provides information about such variation, this article proposes an operational measurement framework for Physiological State (P). P is defined as a latent, multidimensional, and time-dependent configuration generated by ongoing Physiological Organization. Antecedent conditions (A) and consequence-related conditions (C) remain external environmental variables, whereas behavior (B) is modeled as a separate downstream outcome. Rather than uniquely determining behavior, P influences Physiological Accessibility-the state-dependent availability of existing Adaptive Capacities for recruitment and use-and thereby constrains behavioral expression. The construct is distinguished from emotional and cognitive constructs, subjective reports, observable behavior, stress, allostatic load, and individual physiological indicators. Operationalizing requires prespecifying the target behavior and timescale; selecting reliable, sensitive, feasible, and nonredundant physiological indicators; aligning and preprocessing observations; deriving dynamic features; integrating those features through an identifiable latent-state model; representing estimated uncertainty; and conducting prospective validation. The Thirteen Physiological Systems and Seven Layers of Physiological State guide physiological coverage and interpretation but do not correspond one-to-one with the latent dimensions. In a candidate nonlinear state-space implementation, physiological observations, Y(t), provide evidence for estimating P(t), while state evolution depends on preceding P, current A, and relevant prior C. Filtered estimates use only information available through the prediction time. Because B remains outside the physiological observation vector and is evaluated prospectively as B(t + Δ), the framework avoids circularly defining the state by the outcome it is intended to predict. Empirical support would require reliable, interpretable, and temporally coherent state estimates that demonstrate reproducible prospective and incremental value beyond environmental variables, prior behavior, isolated physiological indicators, established single constructs, simple physiological composites, and appropriate linear or lower-dimensional alternatives. Failure to obtain identifiable state estimates or incremental prospective information about B would count against the proposed operationalization. The framework is theoretically and methodologically developmental and should not be interpreted as a validated instrument, diagnostic measure, or universal physiological score.

title: Primary-Tumor Transcriptomic Signatures Associated with Circulating Tumor Cells Status in Breast Cancer: From CTC-Negative Remodeling to CTC-Associated Metastatic Programs
abstract: Background/Objectives: Circulating tumor cells (CTCs) play a central role in metastasis by enabling tumor dissemination through the bloodstream. However, the molecular transition from CTC-negative (CTC-) to CTC-positive (CTC+) states and their associated systemic remodeling remain poorly understood. Methods: We performed a transcriptomic comparison between CTC+, CTC-, and healthy individuals using RNA-seq data and a bioinformatics pipeline. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were subjected to functional enrichment, protein-protein interaction (PPI) analysis, survival modeling, and drug perturbation prediction to delineate the molecular determinants of CTC emergence and persistence. Results: Primary tumors from CTC+ patients exhibited distinct transcriptomic profiles characterized by the upregulation of genes involved in PI3K-Akt signaling, extracellular matrix organization, and chromatin regulation (e.g., HDAC1, JUN, KLK10), alongside the downregulation of immune activation pathways, including complement, B-cell receptor (BCR), and T-cell receptor (TCR) signaling. Multi-gene survival models derived from upregulated (KLK10, MEOX2, IRS4, RND2) and downregulated (ALDH3A1, PPP2R2B, IGF1R) hub genes significantly stratified patient outcomes (HR = 1.74-2.44, p < 0.01). In contrast, primary tumors from CTC- patients displayed early systemic transcriptional alterations relative to healthy controls, with 1700+ DEGs linked to MAPK/ERK and receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) signaling pathways, suggesting pre-metastatic immune reprogramming even before CTC detection. Drug repurposing analysis identified Trichostatin A, BX-795, and Alvocidib as candidate compounds capable of reversing the CTC+ transcriptional signature. Conclusions: Rather than supporting a strictly binary view of CTC status, our findings are consistent with a transcriptional continuum of distinct yet partially overlapping primary-tumor transcriptional states associated with CTC- and CTC+ status, highlighting a molecular shift from immune suppression to epigenetic adaptation that facilitates hematogenous dissemination. The identified multi-gene prognostic panels and small-molecule candidates provide a foundation for CTC-targeted therapeutic strategies and early detection biomarkers in breast cancer.

title: ReCAST: Single-Cell-Informed Tumour Microenvironment Profiling for Translational Prognostic Assessment in Esophageal Cancer.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Single-cell transcriptomics provides detailed maps of the tumour microenvironment, but translating these maps to large clinical cohorts requires methods that can recover biologically meaningful cell states from routinely available bulk transcriptomes and establish whether these states provide information beyond standard clinical factors. The objective of this study was to develop ReCAST, a donor-aware method that estimates tumour microenvironment cell states from bulk tumour transcriptomes, and to test whether these estimates improved survival prediction in esophageal cancer beyond routine clinical variables. Methods: ReCAST constructed outcome-independent cell-state anchors from single-cell transcriptomes by first aggregating expression within donors and then across donors, followed by robust non-negative projection of bulk tumour profiles. The framework was evaluated using synthetic mixtures, 720 genuine-cell pseudo-bulk mixtures from 60 held-out donors, cross-study mixtures from an independent single-cell cohort, an independent adenocarcinoma single-cell cohort, and independently measured tumour compositions in 182 TCGA esophageal cancers. Biological validity was examined against Human Protein Atlas cell-type annotations. ReCAST-derived tumour microenvironment features were subsequently tested for incremental prognostic value beyond age, sex, histology, and stage using repeated cross-validation, and the clinical prediction models were evaluated by locked external validation in an independent cohort of 60 patients with squamous-cell carcinoma. Results: ReCAST recovered 13 biologically coherent cell states whose markers showed strong enrichment for corresponding independent cell-type annotations (fold enrichment 5.1-29.8; FDR -15 ). Cell-state profiles were reproducible across held-out donors and independent studies and donor-aware reference construction improved cross-study transfer. ReCAST outperformed BisqueRNA and unbalanced optimal transport on held-out pseudo-bulk mixtures and, because it worked on within-sample ranks, extended cell-state profiling to data without raw counts, such as variance-stabilised, microarray or summarised reference data; where raw counts were available, count-based methods (MuSiC, DWLS, BayesPrism and a CIBERSORT-type ν-support-vector regression) achieved lower errors and were the preferred complement. In clinical tumours, inferred immune composition tracked independently measured lymphocyte infiltration and leukocyte fraction. Routine clinical variables remained the strongest predictors of survival and were transferred to the independent squamous-cell carcinoma cohort (Uno C-index 0.61); adding ReCAST-derived features produced no incremental improvement (ΔUno C-index -0.033, 95% CI -0.089 to 0.023), a result that was consistent within each histology and with an adenocarcinoma-matched reference. Conclusions: ReCAST provides reproducible cell-state profiles across donors, studies and histologies and extends tumour microenvironment profiling to expression data without raw counts. In esophageal cancer, routine clinical variables already capture the prognostic information carried by cell-state composition, which positions cell-state profiling as a tool for biological characterisation rather than risk prediction. Establishing measurement validity and clinical utility separately provides a robust route for evaluating molecular biomarkers.

title: Gastric Precancerous Progression Beyond the Correa Cascade: Epithelial State Transitions, Microenvironment Remodeling, and Clonal Evolution.
abstract: Gastric carcinogenesis is traditionally framed by the Correa cascade, progressing from chronic inflammation and atrophy through intestinal metaplasia (IM) and dysplasia to carcinoma. Although this model remains clinically useful, it does not fully capture the cellular heterogeneity, molecular diversity, and variable outcomes of gastric precancerous progression. Advances in lineage tracing, organoid models, single-cell sequencing, and spatial omics have revealed multiple metaplastic and transitional epithelial states after mucosal injury, while IM itself comprises distinct cellular and molecular programs rather than a uniform precursor state. Concurrent remodeling of immune and stromal compartments, together with metabolic and stress-related changes, may influence the establishment, maintenance, and adaptation of abnormal epithelial states. Epigenetic alterations, somatic mutations, and clonal expansion further shape the selection of epithelial populations across disease stages. Collectively, current evidence supports a nonlinear model in which epithelial state transitions, microenvironmental remodeling, and molecular and clonal evolution jointly shape gastric precancerous progression. However, much of the available evidence remains cross-sectional, and pseudotime trajectories, spatial proximity, and molecular similarity cannot establish true longitudinal evolution or causality in humans. Future studies should combine standardized spatial sampling, longitudinal follow-up within individuals, functional perturbation, and cross-model validation. Candidate molecular and digital pathology biomarkers should also demonstrate incremental predictive value beyond established histologic and endoscopic risk-stratification systems before they can inform individualized surveillance.

title: Single-Cell Whole-Transcriptome Detection Expands the Observable RNA Space for AI Virtual-Cell Models
abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing has supplied cell atlases and artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled virtual-cell models with scalable, gene-level descriptions of cellular state. Yet prevalent poly(A)-based counting assays capture only part of the RNA landscape. Here, "single-cell whole-transcriptome detection" denotes sequencing-based efforts to detect a broader range of RNA biotypes than conventional poly(A)-based gene counting; no assay detects or quantifies every cellular RNA species without bias. We compare RNA-capture scope, transcript-structure resolution, temporal labeling, spatial context, and additional modalities as distinct measurement dimensions. From a biosensing perspective, analytical sensitivity, transcript coverage, throughput, and assay bias determine which signals are available to computational models. We then examine cell-state representations, regulatory networks, dynamics, perturbation prediction, and foundation models. Total-RNA assays reveal additional non-coding RNAs, long-read methods inform transcript structure, and temporal assays constrain RNA kinetics. Whether these signals improve prediction beyond conventional gene-count inputs requires matched, task-specific model comparisons. We distinguish molecular observability, statistical association, predictive performance, and causal validation, which requires appropriate interventions. We propose benchmarks controlling sequencing depth, cost, model architecture, and held-out samples while testing feature ablations, out-of-distribution performance, uncertainty calibration, and experimental outcomes. Together, high-throughput poly(A)-based profiling and broader RNA measurements provide complementary cellular breadth and regulatory depth.

title: Multi-Omics and Liquid Biopsy Integration for Precision Stratification of Breast Cancer.
abstract: Breast cancer is a biologically heterogeneous disease that requires accurate diagnosis, risk stratification, treatment selection and longitudinal assessment. Conventional imaging and tissue biopsy remain the mainstays of clinical management. However, tissue sampling represents a specific anatomical site and time point, and may not reflect the molecular heterogeneity or evolution of disease. Liquid biopsy offers a minimally invasive complementary approach, analyzing circulating tumor cells (CTCs), circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and extracellular vesicles. Applications include molecular characterization, treatment-response assessment, resistance detection and minimal residual disease (MRD) evaluation, which are under investigation or in clinical use. Gene-expression profiles, mutational alterations and epigenetic marks can generate molecular signatures that offer further support for tumor classification and risk stratification, and have demonstrated clinical value in specific breast cancer populations. Advances in next-generation sequencing, digital PCR, proteomic analysis, and artificial intelligence have expanded the analytical capacity for detection and interpretation of circulating and tissue-derived biomarkers. However, biological heterogeneity, low abundance of circulating biomarkers, pre-analytical and analytical variability, standardization of assays and limited prospective evidence for some applications are still major barriers to clinical translation. In this review, we discuss the biological basis, detection technologies, clinical applications and limitations of liquid biopsies and molecular signatures in breast cancer, highlighting multi-omics integration and computational approaches. It distinguishes between promising analytical biomarkers and clinically validated applications and highlights the evidence and methodological needs for wider implementation in precision breast cancer care.

title: Colorectal Cancer Biomarkers: The Expanding Landscape.
abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains one of the most common malignancies worldwide and a leading cause of cancer-related mortality. Recent advances in CRC molecular biology have focused on biomarkers for early detection, prognostic stratification, treatment selection, and disease monitoring. Clinically validated biomarkers, including microsatellite instability (MSI), RAS and BRAF mutations, HER2 amplification, and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), guide targeted therapy and predict treatment response. However, tumor heterogeneity, clonal evolution, and microenvironmental influences limit the predictive value of single biomarkers. Recent molecular diagnostics therefore increasingly focus on dynamic and minimally invasive approaches. Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) is a promising biomarker for detecting minimal residual disease, monitoring recurrence, and assessing tumor evolution in real time. Multi-omics profiling, spatial transcriptomics, and artificial intelligence further expand tumor characterization except for conventional genomic alterations. Our review integrates common CRC biomarkers with developing liquid biopsy, multi-omics, spatial transcriptomics, and artificial intelligence approaches across early detection, prognosis, treatment selection, and longitudinal monitoring. Future biomarker strategies will likely rely on integrated molecular models combined with longitudinal liquid-biopsy assessment. However, most new biomarkers remain at the investigational stage, and assay heterogeneity, limited standardization, and insufficient prospective clinical validation currently restrict their routine clinical use.

title: Integration of Multi-Omics in AI-Based Models for Predictive Oncology
abstract: Cancer heterogeneity and the emergence of innovative therapeutic alternatives have made the development of tools to help in clinical decision making even more necessary. The recent advances in the field of artificial-intelligence-based predictive models make them promising allies due to their ability to integrate vast amounts of descriptors and data, notably omic data, for grasping cancer complexity. However, it is difficult to present a complete picture of this field due to the increasing number of models and the many possible applications. The aim of this review was to offer an overview of omic-based predictive models in oncology through the prism of three important concepts: the objective, the data, and the model. We show that the consideration of these three aspects could help to assess the feasibility, validity and usability of a model and to guide its construction. Lastly, we highlight that taking into account the underlying technical, physiological and biological phenomena inherent to omic data at each step of the project may improve the model predictive capability and its explainability.

title: Signature Definition Shapes Associations Between Exenatide-Related Transcriptional Programs and Macrophage Senescence Scores in Colorectal Cancer
abstract: Background: Treatment-derived expression signatures are often applied to untreated tumor cohorts, although their biological meaning may depend on signature construction and cellular composition. We examined the relationship between an exenatide-derived signature and senescence-associated macrophage expression in colorectal cancer. Methods: Archived pan-cancer and patient-level results were examined alongside a reconstruction from public mouse bulk RNA sequencing and colorectal single-cell matrices. Exenatide signatures were re-derived with tissue and batch adjustment, within-mouse correlation, and one-to-one orthologue mapping. Shared-gene removal, stricter macrophage annotation, expression-matched random signatures, virtual perturbation summaries, and three murine treatment comparisons assessed interpretation and robustness. Results: The original signature was associated with SenMayo in stomach, colon, and rectal tumor analyses. Reconstruction retained 209,207 colorectal cells and 4316 tumor macrophages, with 17 patients eligible for tumor-level analysis. Removing CXCR2 and IL1B from both signatures preserved a positive association (Spearman ρ = 0.804; adjusted β = 1.526; p = 0.00219). The corresponding mean expression association exceeded most expression-matched random signatures (empirical p = 0.006). Associations persisted with a blocked log-expression derivation but were absent with a blocked voom-derived signature using one-to-one orthologues (ρ = 0.056; p = 0.620). Archived virtual IL1B deletion and overexpression predicted opposing shifts after multiplicity adjustment. Treatment-macrophage fold-change correlations remained small (ρ = -0.038 to 0.046), with heterogeneous enrichment. The association was attenuated after adjustment for either inflammatory score-it remained statistically detectable after TNFα/NF-κB adjustment (β = 0.672, 95% CI 0.307-1.037) and was less precisely estimated after broader inflammatory response adjustment (β = 0.383, 95% CI -0.031-0.797). Conclusions: The original exenatide-derived signature was associated with SenMayo scores in colorectal tumor macrophages after removal of shared genes. This association overlapped with inflammatory expression and varied with signature derivation. Dependence on signature derivation limits its interpretation as a pharmacological response marker. These findings support investigation of inflammatory macrophage states without establishing drug-induced senescence.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Plant Gene Regulatory Networks.
abstract: Gene regulatory networks (GRNs) are the maps that plant biologists most want to draw, with arrows pointing from transcription factors to the genes they control, explaining how plants develop and respond to the environment. Since experimental validation of even one arrow can take years, and a single plant genome harbours tens of millions of candidate TF-target pairs, this gap has driven the development of numerous computational methods for GRN inference. Here I review three generations of computational approaches to plant GRN inference and measure them against a five-level ladder of evidence, including statistical association, conditional dependence, physical binding, functional regulation and causal circuits. Classical statistics and machine learning have simplified complex gene expression data into clear, prioritised predictions. Techniques like single-cell and multi-omics methods help uncover cell type-specific networks based on chromatin accessibility and binding motifs. Now, deep learning can interpret cis-regulatory grammar directly from genome sequences, and foundation models trained on plant genomes and millions of cells hold exciting potential to share regulatory insights across different species. The most promising route forward is a lab-in-the-loop division of labour in which foundation models serve not as oracles but as hypothesis engines, collapsing fifty million candidate TF-target pairs into the few hundred edges most worth the bench's time, with each round of validation sharpening the next round of prediction.

title: A Multimodal Arrayed CRISPRi Framework for Functional Characterization of lncRNAs Across Cellular Contexts.
abstract: Background : Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) are numerous, often lowly expressed, and highly context-dependent, making their functional characterization challenging using single-readout approaches. Integrating target repression assessment with complementary molecular and cellular phenotyping is therefore important for systematic lncRNA functional characterization across cellular contexts. Methods : To address this, we developed an arrayed CRISPR interference (CRISPRi)-based multimodal framework for functional lncRNA characterization across cellular contexts, pairing targeted knockdown with target repression assessment, shallow 3'-end RNA-seq, live-cell growth analysis, and Cell Painting-based morphological profiling. As a proof of concept, we applied this strategy to HEK293T and KELLY cells, targeting 68 expressed lncRNAs. Results : Targeted 3'-end RNA capture-seq stratified targets by baseline coverage and confirmed measurable repression for 18 lncRNAs in HEK293T cells and 21 lncRNAs in KELLY cells. Transcriptomic profiling captured the broadest layer of downstream response to lncRNA repression, whereas growth and morphology phenotypes were less frequent and restricted to a small subset of targets. Matched comparisons between HEK293T and KELLY showed that both molecular and cellular responses to the same lncRNA perturbation were often cell-line-dependent. As a representative multimodal hit, EPB41L4A-AS1 repression in KELLY cells was associated with reduced translation- and biosynthesis-related pathway activity, reduced cell growth, and morphological feature changes involving Golgi, actin and mitochondria. Conclusions : Together, these results demonstrate that arrayed CRISPRi coupled with multimodal profiling provides a structured framework for systematically characterizing lncRNA perturbation effects across complementary molecular and cellular readouts and prioritizing candidate functional lncRNAs for downstream mechanistic studies.

title: Artificial intelligence in cancer transcriptomics: methods, applications in oncology, and limitations
abstract: Background. Transcriptomic data show which genes are active in cells and tissues. Machine-learning and deep-learning methods use these data to classify samples, integrate different datasets, and predict biological properties and treatment response. In oncology, a major challenge is transferring patterns identified in experimental models to tumor samples from patients. Objective. To critically synthesize current artificial-intelligence methods for transcriptomic analysis, with emphasis on oncology applications, transfer of models to patient data, and requirements for clinical validation. Materials and Methods. We performed a critical narrative review of primary studies and methodological papers and additionally described the authors' publication sample for 2021–2026. The literature review was updated through August 13, 2026. Results. The most developed areas include single-cell data analysis, spatially resolved tumor diagnostics, and drug-response prediction. Independent comparative evaluations show that increasing model size and complexity does not guarantee better performance than simpler methods. Clinical translation requires accounting for cellular composition and technical differences between measurement batches, aligning experimental and clinical response measures, preventing information leakage, and performing external validation. Conclusion. Artificial intelligence should be viewed as a data-analysis tool rather than a substitute for experimental or clinical validation. Its value depends on data quality, correct task definition, and the ability to maintain performance in independent cohorts.

title: Decoding proteomic complexity of transcript variants and homologous isoforms for precision therapeutics
abstract: The traditional "one gene, one protein" paradigm is insufficient to capture the vast phenotypic and physiological complexity of eukaryotes. This review aims to comprehensively elucidate the molecular mechanisms of transcriptomic diversification, namely, alternative splicing, alternative usage of promoter, and alternative polyadenylation, and their profound impacts on cellular homeostasis and human disease. By synthesizing recent breakthroughs in targeted long-read RNA sequencing, single-cell isoform-specific multiomics, and AI-driven 3D structural modeling, we systematically examine how transcript variants are generated and functionally annotated. Our analysis highlights that multiple transcript variants originating from a single genetic locus are not merely redundant copies; rather, subtle sequence alterations dynamically rewire protein-protein interaction networks and dictate precise subcellular localization. The exquisite spatiotemporal regulation of these variants controls critical cell fate decisions and organ development. Consequently, the pathological dysregulation of these processes, frequently termed spliceopathies, acts as a primary driver in severe pathologies, including cancer multidrug resistance, metabolic reprogramming, and neurodegenerative disorders. In conclusion, understanding the eukaryotic proteome requires a fundamental shift from conventional gene-level to isoform-level perspectives. Decoding the complex regulatory syntax of transcript variants paves the way for next-generation precision medicine, highlighting the therapeutic potential of RNA-targeted interventions, such as antisense oligonucleotides and CRISPR-based RNA editing, to correct pathogenic isoforms.

title: Reproducibility code for the scVelo–RegVelo quantitative reanalysis of zebrafish neural crest cell fate
abstract: This repository provides the reproducibility code for the quantitative reanalysis reported in the review “From Cellular Variability to Predictive Cell-Fate Modeling: Preprocessing, Dynamic Inference, and Perturbation Validation.” The workflow reproduces the scVelo–RegVelo comparison in a published zebrafish neural crest dataset, including matched 1,008-gene and official 988-gene terminal-state identification analyses, developmental-stage concordance, RegVelo in silico transcription-factor perturbation, comparison with Perturb-seq measurements, exact TF-block permutation testing, bootstrap and leave-one-TF-out robustness analyses, and combined-kernel sensitivity analysis. The workflow starts from publicly available inputs and regenerates the processed objects and quantitative results used in the manuscript.
affiliations: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Code and processed results for: Decluttering Tree Models via Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization
abstract: This record accompanies the manuscript "Decluttering Tree Models via Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization." It contains original Python analysis scripts, processed benchmark and biological results, small public benchmark caches, Figures 1–8, and graphical-abstract/eTOC materials. Version v3 (R5 corrected package) adds corrected PBMC, DepMap BRAF, and Perturb-seq SNAI1 analyses; fixed-K and all-K validation paths; updated gene-signature and external-validation tables; and the corresponding figures. It retains the validation-selected selector comparisons, paired split-level results, and scaling checks through 1,000 trees from the preceding version. README.md and RUN_REPRODUCTION.md provide reproduction instructions. Large third-party raw datasets and private API credentials are excluded. Original code is licensed under MIT, original processed results under CC0, and original manuscript text and figures under CC BY 4.0; third-party datasets retain their own terms.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Analysis package for A detectability floor for treatment-response labels in rheumatology transcriptomics
abstract: Deposit for the manuscript "A detectability floor for treatment-response labels inrheumatology transcriptomics". The archive contains everything needed to reproduce thereported numbers from public input data; no new data were generated and no controlled-accessmaterial was used. Contents: data provenance for the extended label audit (platform, annotation priority, genecoverage, retrieval date, label field and mapping rule, deposited-versus-published group-sizecomparison); the pre-registered audit protocol; per-sample response labels recovered from eachdeposit; the screening and adjudication ledgers taking 45 auditable papers down to 15 auditedcohorts, with a registered reason for every exclusion; the analysis and plotting code for theprimary cohorts (juvenile dermatomyositis, rheumatoid arthritis before/after methotrexate,lupus nephritis, two controlled glucocorticoid challenges, a single-cell dose series), thegender-composition and per-gene stability checks, the score-level injection calibration andthe attainable-AUC ceiling analysis; and the corresponding result files. Design floors are exact non-central-t minima (80% power, two-sided alpha = 0.05) computed foreach cohort from its own group sizes, so a negative result is reported as a bound rather thanan absence. Verdicts follow a taxonomy that was registered before any verdict was computed.A verdict characterises the detectability of a supervision label as deposited; it is not aclaim that any published analysis was erroneous. No virtual-cell model was evaluated in thiswork. Language convention: file names, field names, column headers, verdict codes and all numericoutput are in English. Recorded screening reasons, adjudication notes and analysis logannotations are in the authors' working language (Chinese); the full PRISMA-style screeningrecord is deposited in its original form with an English summary prepended, and every ledgeris described in ledgers/README_ledgers.md.
affiliations: First Affiliated Hospital of Gannan Medical University

title: Benchmarking single-cell foundation models for aging biology
abstract: This benchmark evaluates how single-cell foundation models capture aging-related information in cell and gene representations. It compares ten foundation models with aging-specific methods and conventional baselines across five tasks: chronological-age prediction, age-associated trajectory reconstruction, disease-associated age shifts, senescent-cell identification, and regulatory-edge recovery. Evaluations span human and mouse data, with validation across donors, datasets, experimental domains and species where applicable. Together, these tasks assess the predictive utility, generalization and biological information of pretrained representations across complementary aspects of aging.

title: HeteroSC benchmark data: processed single-cell annotation datasets, drug-response tables, perturbation splits and data partitions
abstract: HeteroSC benchmark data: the datasets, processed tables and data partitions behind "Can Heterogeneous Single-Cell Foundation Models Work Better Together? HeteroSC for Adapter-Based Integration and Orchestration of Complementary ScFM Experts". HeteroSC combines four frozen single-cell foundation models (Geneformer, scGPT, CellFM and scFoundation) through expert-specific adapters and an input-dependent AdaptiveRouter. It is tested on three tasks: cell type annotation, gene perturbation prediction and unseen-drug response prediction. This record holds the data side of those experiments. What's inside (three archives, each keeping the folder layout used by the code) annotation: five scRNA-seq datasets (Pancreas, Skin, Liver, Lung, Myeloid) as original and processed .h5ad files, plus the exact train/validation/test assignment of every cell (stratified 70/15/15, seed 42, shared by all four models). drug_response: 109,152 cell line–drug pairs covering 551 cell lines and 223 drugs, with GDSC AUC as the target. Includes a 10-fold leave-drug-out partition where every drug sits in exactly one fold, drug graph and fingerprint features, CCLE expression of 697 genes, and the DepMap mapping file. gene_perturbation: Norman and Adamson Perturb-seq data in GEARS format, the GEARS simulation split used in the study (seed 3, train_gene_set_size 0.75) and GEARS' auxiliary GO resources. Not included: foundation-model embeddings, trained weights and pretrained checkpoints (all reproducible with the code), and the raw GDSC dose-response files, which should be downloaded from cancerrxgene.org under GDSC's terms. Terms and attribution: author-generated files (partitions, fold assignments, summaries) are released under CC BY 4.0. Third-party data keep the licences and terms of their original providers, so please cite the original publications, notably Norman et al. 2019, Adamson et al. 2016 and Roohani et al. 2024 (GEARS), Yang et al. 2013 and Iorio et al. 2016 (GDSC), and Barretina et al. 2012 and Ghandi et al. 2019 (CCLE). GDSC-derived values follow the GDSC data usage policy; DepMap data are generally CC BY 4.0. Code: https://github.com/kit-cml/HeteroSC_code.git Citation: Nursyafi FS, Hanum UL, Fuadah YN, Lim KM. Can Heterogeneous Single-Cell Foundation Models Work Better Together? HeteroSC for Adapter-Based Integration and Orchestration of Complementary ScFM Experts. Manuscript under review.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Liatir Single-Cell Foundation Model Benchmark — Reproducibility Compendium
abstract: This record contains the complete reproducibility compendium for the Liatir single-cell foundation-model benchmark. The study compares established single-cell representation and integration methods (PCA, Harmony and scVI) with zero-shot embeddings from Geneformer V1 10M and scGPT whole-human on two public scRNA-seq datasets: PBMC (11,990 cells) and the scIB Pancreas integration benchmark (16,382 cells). UCE 4-layer was included in the experimental design but could not be evaluated: the PBMC run exceeded the approved memory limit on the original host, while no signed Linux Runtime Box was available for the Pancreas execution environment. The evaluation covers clustering agreement, cell-type separability and classification, batch integration, runtime, memory usage and execution provenance. Across these two datasets, pretrained foundation-model representations did not show a uniform advantage over established baselines. scGPT was competitive on PBMC, while PCA, Harmony and scVI remained particularly strong on Pancreas. The study was executed through Liatir's native Jobs and Results system. The compendium contains the frozen study code, prepared scientific inputs, embeddings, configurations, environment records, provenance, telemetry, result tables, figures, validation evidence and reproduction utilities required to inspect and independently recompute the reported biological and batch metrics. Independent evaluation reproduction matched all completed reported metrics within absolute tolerance 1e-9 and relative tolerance 1e-8. Source identities, cell and gene ordering, evaluation splits and generated representations are preserved through recorded checksums. This record is intended as a reproducibility artifact and scientific showcase rather than evidence of general statistical superiority between methods. The study uses two datasets and one evaluation seed, and computational timings were produced on heterogeneous hardware for some configurations. Study implementation and execution used AI-assisted coding support alongside human work and under human direction; all reported measurements derive from recorded executions and reproducibility checks.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Supporting Information LCA Battery Pack Production
abstract: This dataset contains the underlying numerical results, life cycle inventory (LCI) data and cell bill of material supporting the manuscript "Material and Supply Chain Pathways Shaping the Environmental Impact of Lithium- and Sodium-Ion Battery Packs". The dataset comprises three parts: LCA Results: Numerical impact assessment results for all 27 battery pack configurations analyzed in the study, including a process-chain resolved breakdown of contributions from individual production steps such as anode active material, cathode active material, electrode manufacturing, cell assembly, and pack integration. Results are provided for all impact categories reported in the manuscript. Life Cycle Inventories (LCI): Input flow data used within the modeling framework, specifying the material and energy inputs associated with each process step in the sequential production chain.Cell Bill of Materials (Cell BOM): Component-wise material masses for every modeled cell, derived from the ICPD design parameters and resolved into anode, cathode, electrolyte, separator, and cell assembly sub-inventories. The Cell BOM forms the interface between the virtual cell design and the life cycle modeling.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: The autism risk-protein interactome marks neuronal perturbation sensitivity across functional scales
abstract: This dataset accompanies the study entitled "The autism risk-protein interactome marks neuronal perturbation sensitivity across functional scales." The study investigates the functional relevance of experimentally identified interaction partners of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) risk proteins by integrating protein–protein interaction networks with neuronal CRISPR-based perturbation screens, human cortical-neuron Perturb-seq, mouse in vivo neuronal dependency data, and transcriptomic evidence from ASD postmortem cortex. This repository contains curated analysis outputs and supporting data associated with the study, including: Summary data underlying selected main and supplementary figure panels. Statistical results and sensitivity analyses, including supplementary analysis tables. Data supporting the evaluation of baseline expression and gene essentiality as potential confounding factors. DepMap Public 24Q4 common-essential gene annotations. Data dictionaries, source information, and provenance records. These materials are provided to facilitate transparent reporting, interpretation, and reuse of the study's analytical results. The archive contains selected aggregate results and figure-source summaries rather than the complete raw datasets or all gene-level inputs required to rerun the original statistical analyses. Original third-party data remain subject to their respective source licenses and attribution requirements.

title: Preregistration: Would US Adults on an Online Panel Donate Tissue for AI Training? A Four-Version Split-Ballot Survey
abstract: What this is A preregistration of a survey, published before any data were collected. It fixes the questions, hypotheses, exclusions, analysis code and decision rules in public before the pilot launches. Survey privacy notice: privacy-notice.pdf. This is the notice the survey introduction links to; the same text is part 4 of preregistration.pdf. Purpose Some consent forms for medical research, such as the Human Cell Atlas template, say donated tissue data may be used "for any purpose". The survey asks US adults whether they would agree to donate a small sample of tissue or cells for medical research when told the data could be used to train artificial intelligence (AI) models, by whom, and with a one-year period of first use by companies. Design A four-version split ballot. Each respondent is assigned at random to one description of how the data could be used: by university and hospital researchers by university and hospital researchers to train AI models by companies to train AI models by companies to train AI models, with only those companies able to use the data for the first year, after which it is made available to the public The question that follows is word for word the same in all four versions. An attention check comes first; four follow-up questions and four background questions come after. 10 questions in all. Sample US adults 18 and over in the Pollfish online panel (panel vendor: Pollfish LLC). An opt-in panel, not a probability sample. Planned: a 40-complete pilot, never pooled; then 1,000 completes, about 250 per version. Budget Hard cap of $2,000 for pilot and main survey together, paid by SuperTruth Inc. If the price is higher than planned, the survey buys fewer completes. Preregistered contrasts Outcome: the share answering "Definitely would" or "Probably would". H1 (primary): version 4 lower than version 1. H2: version 3 lower than version 1. H3: version 4 lower than version 3. H2 and H3 are tested only if H1 is a finding, with Holm's correction. Version 2 against 1 and version 3 against 2 are exploratory, with intervals only. Where a comparison changes more than one thing at once, every result names all of the changes. Results Reported whichever way they fall, using the sentences written in advance for each outcome (preregistration.pdf, part 1, section 10), including a result against our hypotheses. Privacy The authors receive no names, contact details or device IDs. No question asks about health. The public response file holds only the version seen, answers to the first six questions and the exclusion reason, with no ID. The raw export stays on one SuperTruth computer and is deleted within 90 days of the report and public file being published, and by 31 December 2027 at the latest. Ethics No IRB review. In the authors' judgment this is a minimal-risk opinion survey with no federal funding. Funding and conflicts SuperTruth Inc. pays for the fieldwork. SuperTruth develops data-trust technology; a finding that people tell research uses apart would support that business. The authors wrote the questions and the directional hypotheses. MedSync supplies no money, staff, data or facilities for the survey. Files preregistration.pdf: the full preregistration. privacy-notice.pdf: the survey privacy notice. analyze.py, test_analyze.py, make_synthetic.py: analysis code and tests. README.txt: file list with SHA-256 checksums. Companion paper "Data Truth Is AI Truth: Provenance and Consent in the Data Behind the $1.8 Billion Virtual Cell" (in preparation).
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: NDVPP JGG V2: Code and Source Data for Response-Offset Calibration in Cross-Cell Perturbation Prediction
abstract: Real saved code and frozen source data for the manuscript “Response-offset calibration can reduce error without target-specific utility in perturbation prediction”. Includes Mean-only sensitivity (Table S13), bidirectional intercept-only residual-offset calibration on 1,588 TRAIN / 397 TEST targets (Figure 4B/Table S14), calibration sizes n=25/50/100/200 with 20 fixed seeds (Figure 4C-D/Table S15), and a separate exploratory 1,985-target five-fold OOF comparison of Ridge, MLP and LightGBM. No fitting, tuning or resampling was rerun during packaging. Archived scripts require their original directory layouts and reconciliation of documented path/newline transformations and original-hash assertions. Full per-unit models, original offline venv and all raw-to-paper historical intermediates are not included; complete clean-room numerical replay is not claimed. Plotting adapters are distinct from original statistical executors. The historical 397 TEST task is outcome-exposed and is not independent sealed validation. Historical DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22074841 covers older code only; this independent expanded V2 package includes later analyses. Funding: National Natural Science Foundation of China, 82374226. Author-owned code is licensed under the MIT License; author-owned redistributable derived results are licensed under CC BY 4.0; third-party material retains its original terms. The mixed-source descriptor matrix and source_data/posthoc_multimodel/INPUTS.npz are excluded because redistribution terms are not established; retrieval paths and hashes are documented in DATA_SOURCES.md and provenance/RELEASE_LICENSE_EXCLUSIONS.tsv.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: EL-RAKHAWI DOCTRINE OF QUANTUM CELLULAR DIGITAL TWINS A UNIFIED MATHEMATICAL FRAMEWORK FOR WHOLE-CELL HUMAN SIMULATION AND IN-SILICO CLINICAL TRIALS
abstract: EL-RAKHAWI DOCTRINE OF QUANTUM CELLULAR DIGITAL TWINS: SUMMARY This revolutionary framework presents a unified mathematical approach for whole-cell human simulation and in-silico clinical trials, addressing fundamental limitations in drug discovery and biological research. Four foundational pillars: (1) Cellular Coherence Equation (ECCE) - A conceptual coupling framework using hybrid state descriptors that unifies quantum mechanics, metabolic flux, gene regulation, and epigenetic matrices across multiple mathematical subspaces (Hilbert and Euclidean spaces) with dynamic boundary conditions. (2) Dynamic Delegation Algorithm - Real-time computational fidelity switching between QM (quantum mechanics), MD (molecular dynamics), and FBA (flux balance analysis) based on event relevance thresholds, incorporating smooth adaptive energy handoff protocols (ONIOM-based) to ensure numerical stability and force continuity during multi-scale transitions. (3) Phase 0 In-Silico Clinical Trials - Population-scale digital twin simulations (1,000,000 virtual cells representing global genetic diversity/SNPs) predicting drug efficacy, toxicity, and resistance in 48 hours, reducing development timeline from 10 years to 18 months and costs by 90%. (4) Federated Learning with Quantum-Secure Communication - Privacy-preserving architecture using post-quantum cryptography (CRYSTALS-Kyber/Dilithium) and quantum key distribution (QKD) for secure gradient aggregation across distributed hospital networks, ensuring HIPAA/GDPR compliance. Economic impact: Reduces drug development cost from $2.6B to $200-400M, improves success rate from 10% to 40-50%, generates $50-80B annual revenue potential with 1000-3000% ROI. Ironclad intellectual property protection covering 6 patent applications under Berne Convention, PCT, and TRIPS, with perpetual moral rights and trade secret protection. title: CellPert: source code and trained model weights
abstract: Source code and trained model weights for CellPert, a graph-structured variational autoencoder with biological priors for cross-platform chemical perturbation prediction, accompanying the article "CellPert: Graph-based variational learning with biological priors for cross-dataset perturbation prediction" (Patterns). CellPert-main.zip is a snapshot of the GitHub repository https://github.com/QSong-github/CellPert (main branch, commit 31096305df8210a1ed45dff856015ac03e0be672). best_gin_vae_model_node_level.pth is the trained checkpoint used for all results reported in the article (MD5 3c766013e5fb949ff77fb047c296a093). Installation and usage instructions are in the README of the repository.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

llm.why_it_matters_zh: 公开代码与权重便于复用，对化学扰动预测的复现和扩展有直接价值。
llm.limitations_zh: 摘要未提及。

title: CellPert: processed LINCS L1000 and Mini Tahoe-100M datasets
abstract: Processed datasets used to train and evaluate CellPert, accompanying the article "CellPert: Graph-based variational learning with biological priors for cross-dataset perturbation prediction" (Patterns). lincs.zip contains the LINCS L1000 chemical-perturbation training data (GEO GSE70138, Level 3) restricted to the 965 genes shared with Mini Tahoe-100M, with compound Morgan fingerprints (AnnData .h5ad), together with the preprocessed graph data chunks read by CellPert. minitahoe.tar.gz contains the Mini Tahoe-100M evaluation data, 14 plates derived from Tahoe-100M (https://huggingface.co/datasets/tahoebio/Tahoe-100M), with one AnnData .h5ad file per plate restricted to the same 965 genes, together with the preprocessed graph data chunks. The source code and trained model weights are archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23329393. Usage instructions are in the README of https://github.com/QSong-github/CellPert.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Pseudo-bulk knock-out profiles from the in vivo whole-brain Perturb-seq atlas of Shi et al. (2026), used in RFind-sc
abstract: For each of five neuronal cell types, the UMI counts of the nuclei of each column (a knock-out, a safe-targeting control or the non-targeting control) of the in vivo whole-brain Perturb-seq atlas of Shi et al. (2026; Hugging Face perturbai/wholebrain_crispr_atlas, commit a7c65dc0a64da4bd47cf6ef5f4dec6c7ef745e87, CC BY 4.0) were summed gene by gene. These profiles are the knock-out references of Fig. 4, Supplementary Fig. S3 and Supplementary Tables 1 and 2 of "RFind-sc maps single cells onto biological axes defined by expression signatures and genetic perturbations" (Murano and Miyakawa). Files: pb_g017_DG.npz (DG Glut), pb_CA1.npz (CA1 Glut), pb_g017_CA3.npz (CA3 Glut), pb_GABA3.npz (GABAergic neurons: Pvalb, Sst and Lamp5 summed) and pb_g151.npz (151 TH Prkcd Grin2c Glut). Each NumPy .npz file (numpy.load(path, allow_pickle=False)) holds counts (19,070 genes x 2,046-2,048 columns, float32), genes (gene symbols), targets (the targeted gene or control of each column) and n_cells (the number of nuclei in each column). The code that makes and uses these files is at https://github.com/tmurano/RFind-sc.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

new_dataset_names: Pseudo-bulk knock-out profiles of the whole-brain Perturb-seq atlas

title: Microrobotic Quantum Causal Tomography of Disease Microenvironments at the Limit An intervention-aware architecture for distinguishing mechanisms from spatial association Core coupling Spatially targeted microsampling × quantum multimodal readout × causal inversion Research scale 30 linked derivations × 82 chapters × 410 research sections × 200 detailed Research Gates Main result A testable route from spatial biomarker maps to intervention-tested mechanism candidates, while preserving unresolved equivalence when evidence cannot identify direction. Mother lineage Microrobotic Sampling and Quantum Biosensing Co-Design at the Limit Publication Abstract This monograph asks whether microrobotic samples collected across position, depth, and time can support causal discrimination within disease microenvironments rather than merely produce biomarker heatmaps. The scientific object is the complete chain linking tissue state, transport, sampling path, probe footprint, multimodal measurement, candidate causal graph, local intervention, and held-out outcome. Spatial proximity, predictive accuracy, and cross-modal agreement do not establish direction when position, batch, cell composition, measurement error, or common calibration can explain the same pattern. The framework treats causal tomography as an uncertainty-bearing inverse problem that may remain non-unique. Tumor, chronic-inflammation, and fibrotic microenvironments are evaluated as separate test platforms. The central falsifiable proposition is that a safe, local, reversible perturbation should distinguish at least some mechanisms that generate the same terminal phenotype. If intervention data do not separate the models, if conclusions are prior dominated, or if sampling changes the disease state, the result is downgraded to a descriptive atlas or an unresolved equivalence class. Scientific Position and Hard Boundary A high-resolution map is not automatically a mechanism map. A microrobot can deplete analytes, redistribute fluid, compress matrix, alter local temperature, create adsorption memory, or preferentially reach some regions. Quantum sensing can improve selected measurements, but it can also add optical, thermal, magnetic, preparation, and readout costs. These effects enter the causal model as measured variables and uncertainty sources rather than disappearing behind the terms minimally invasive or quantum enhanced. Candidate Research Expression Cmicro = Iid Across Rintervention − Eequiv − Dsampling − Bprior • Iid measures the identifiability of the declared causal parameters. • Across measures agreement across genuinely informative and independently referenced modalities. • Rintervention measures agreement between predicted and observed responses to a held-out local intervention. • Eequiv measures the remaining set of observationally or interventionally equivalent models. • Dsampling measures distortion caused by the sampling path, footprint, depletion, carryover, or tissue contact. • Bprior measures how strongly the conclusion is supplied by prior assumptions or regularization. Authorization, tissue safety, irreversible harm, missing raw evidence, broken sample identity, and failed independent references are hard vetoes. No favorable score can cancel them. Five-Layer Research Architecture 01 Disease-Specific Causal Contract Declare the disease platform, causal estimand, intervention semantics, competing mechanisms, evidence tier, and conditions that force an unresolved answer. 02 Spatial Sampling and Disturbance Physics Measure coordinates, depth, time, route, probe footprint, transport, depletion, carryover, tissue displacement, and recovery. 03 Quantum Multimodal Evidence Preserve raw quantum and classical channels, selectivity, shared covariance, matrix effects, calibration ancestry, and measurement backaction. 04 Identification and Counterfactual Testing Audit confounding, selection, measurement error, latent variables, positivity, equivalence, partial identification, and held-out intervention prediction. 05 External Validation and Successor Choice Test new lots, sites, operators, and disease-specific platforms; reconstruct without the creator; and permit rejection, simplification, or retirement. Minimum Verifiable Prototype Construct a tissue-chip system in which two mechanisms produce a similar terminal biomarker pattern. Hide the mechanism labels and randomize sampling route, location, perturbation amplitude, and timing. Compare fixed sampling, descriptive spatial profiling, and microrobot-guided active discrimination under matched tissue, time, energy, sample-volume, and analysis budgets. Freeze the causal prediction before revealing ground truth. An independent assay then determines whether the system identified the mechanism, merely memorized position or batch, or changed the state it attempted to explain. Research Contributions • Separates spatial association, prediction, partial identification, and intervention-suppor

title: Single-cell morpho-molecular foundation modeling from histopathology with PAST
abstract: We present PAST, a single-cell morpho-molecular foundation model trained on ~20 million paired single-cell image–transcriptome instances derived from 49 tissue sections, comprising 42 human sections from 40 independent patients and 7 mouse sections across 15 tumor and tissue contexts. By jointly encoding cellular morphology and gene expression, PAST learns unified cross-modal representations that capture both spatial and molecular heterogeneity at the cellular level, enabling accurate prediction of single-cell gene expression, virtual molecular staining, and multimodal survival analysis directly from routine pathology slides.

title: Data Truth Is AI Truth: Provenance and Consent in the Data Behind the $1.8 Billion Virtual Cell
abstract: A working paper about who agreed to what in the data behind the 1.8 billion dollar Virtual Biology Initiative, the October 2026 American effort to build open data for AI models of human cells. What this is Funders include the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative and Biohub, the US Department of Energy, the National Institutes of Health, plus Google DeepMind, Isomorphic Labs and Meta, who put in 300 million dollars with a year of exclusive access to the data. A working paper, not yet peer-reviewed. We asked every organization named for comment: the Human Cell Atlas answered in full, the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative replied it had no comment after reading the draft, and the rest are noted as asked. All author quotes printed with approval; one cited-study author reviewed in background and is unnamed per her terms. What it finds None of the official announcements mentions donor consent or data provenance, the record of where data came from. No AI-training-use field in CELLxGENE, the Human Cell Atlas schema, the NIH archives, or the standard consent codes; the consent texts read do not mention AI or embargo. The Human Cell Atlas gap in 2025 and 2026, shown beside the Atlas's own schema-migration explanation. A preregistered survey of 963 Americans: support falls about 18 points when data goes to company AI behind an embargo rather than university researchers; limits stated at length. Closes with seven requests to the initiative, starting with writing consent down where machines can read it. Files The full manuscript as PDF, previewed above. z-data.zip: the complete deposit behind the paper (manuscript text, 3,512 redacted repository listings, counts, survey files, methods, code); repo paths preserved inside.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
